title: Latent Error — rich
forward_vector: I am the manifest of Latent Error's rich face, its first round at Sketch tier, a proposal: two made walks, each turning the page's own method on the page. Holes that line up asks what the Swiss cheese model takes for granted, that the layers fail on their own, and measures what a shared condition costs; the room that settles short asks what the PID section takes for granted, and finds it ran steady-state error and oscillation together. I grow toward the teaching and tool-design cases the page names, measured the same way. I never hold the entry's words.

offers.section: Control Theory Translation: The Integral Term
offers.what: The section runs together two failures. Steady-state error is a loop that settles off the target; oscillation is a loop that never settles, and it comes from lag, not from P alone. The room that settles short measured it. Room: 10-minute lag, 5 °C outside, target 20 °C, a window open from minute 60. In a room that answers at once, P alone never overshoots at any gain (Kp 0.05 to 5: overshoot 0.00 °C) and settles short by (20 − 5 + 5) ÷ (1 + 30·Kp): 17.14 °C at Kp 0.2, 19.87 at Kp 5. Give it a 2-minute radiator and a 1-minute thermometer and P alone swings without end from Kp ≈ 0.66, by Routh and by the run. Even then the swing is centred on P's offset, not the target: at Kp 0.7 it goes 18.24 to 19.91 °C and never reaches 20. Of eight runs, the one the page's sentence describes ('oscillate around the target, never settling') has an I term: Kp 0.2, Ki 0.07 swings 18.28 to 21.54. Likewise 'A system with I term will converge' holds only below a bound, about Ki 0.063 at Kp 0.2 here. Suggested, for the P paragraph: 'This alone leaves an offset: P needs some error to keep acting, so the system settles short of the target. In a system with lag, a high P also overshoots and can swing without end, still centred short of the target.' For the paragraph after 'Latent error thinking is the I term': 'A system with P but no I term will always settle off the target. A system with a modest I term converges on it; too much I overshoots, and with lag it can oscillate on its own.' The second half is a tension worth holding rather than smoothing: memory pushed too hard overshoots, which bears on the 'In life' reading too.

'Redesign so failure requires more than one simultaneous mistake' holds only when those mistakes can't share a cause, and the page doesn't say so. Holes that line up measured it. Three slices with 15% holes promise 0.34% through. If one shared condition lines the holes up a quarter of the time (β 0.25), 4.00% gets through, twelve times the promise: the stack acts like 1.70 independent slices. A fourth slice of the same design brings that only to 3.79%. Redesigning one slice so the condition can't reach it brings it to 0.82%. With no shared condition (β 0), the extra slice wins and the redesign changes nothing. All of this is 200,000 counted hazards per run, matching β·p + (1 − β)·pⁿ. Suggested, after the last sentence: '… more than one simultaneous mistake, and so those mistakes can't share a cause: layers that fail for the same reason count as one.' The same count also gives Open Question 1 a first measure: how many independent layers a stack really acts like, n_eff = log P ÷ log p, against how many it has.

A fact to check, found by reading, not by a piece. The classic case is usually told as landing gear and flaps, not ejection and landing gear. Alphonse Chapanis found identical toggle switches for the two side by side in the B-17, and fixed it by shape coding: a wheel-shaped knob for the gear, a wedge for the flaps. I found no ejection-lever version. Suggested, if Loudon confirms the source he had in mind: 'identical-looking controls for landing gear and flaps (the B-17 case Alphonse Chapanis studied in the 1940s)'. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alphonse_Chapanis. The point the example makes, design not attention, is unchanged.

pieces.title: Holes that line up · the Swiss cheese model, counted
pieces.caption:
**What does the Swiss cheese model take for granted?** Four steps, no sound. First, one slice with one hole: the share of hazards that get through is the size of the hole. Then a stack whose holes wander on their own: three slices with 15% holes let 0.34% through. Then a condition every slice shares, like two identical-looking levers that fool the eye, the checklist and the habit all the same way. When it is in play, the holes line up. At a quarter of the time, three slices let 4.0% through and act like 1.7 independent ones, and no number of slices of the same design gets under 3.75%. Last, the page's advice measured on 200,000 hazards each way. Adding a fourth slice of the same design gives 3.79%. Redesigning one slice so the condition can't reach it gives 0.82%. With no shared condition, the extra slice wins instead.

P = β·p + (1 − β)·pⁿ   ·   n_eff = log P ÷ log p

(share through) = (the time one condition shapes every slice) × (one hole) + (the rest of the time) × (every hole lining up by chance); (how many independent slices it acts like) = log of the share through ÷ log of one hole

pieces.title: The room that settles short · P, I and D on a heated room
pieces.caption:
**Does P alone oscillate, or settle short?** Six steps on a heated room: 5 °C outside, a target of 20, a window that opens at minute 60. First the room alone, with the heater set by hand. Then P in a room that answers at once: at any gain it settles short of 20 and never overshoots. Then the lag a real radiator and thermometer have: now a high P overshoots, and past Kp ≈ 0.66 it swings forever, but around the offset line, below the target, never reaching 20 at Kp 0.7. Then I, whose memory pulls the room onto 20 and at rest carries all of the heat, and which overshoots in its turn when there is too much of it. Then D: a little calms the ringing, a lot brings the overshoot back. Last, the page's own sentence against eight runs. Its first half holds for every P-alone run. Its second half fits only a run with an I term. *Hear it* plays the room as a tone beside the target's: an offset is a beat that never stops, an oscillation a beat that never holds still.

u = Kp·e + Ki·∫e dt − Kd·dS/dt   ·   P alone rests short by (20 − 5 + 5) ÷ (1 + 30·Kp)

(the heater's share) = Kp × (the error now) + Ki × (all the error so far) − Kd × (how fast the thermometer is rising); with P alone, the room rests short of the target by 20 degrees of loss ÷ (1 + 30 × Kp)
